title: Drugs changed Welton, say friends, family
article: Only once, said Carroll Welton, did he see his son, Derek, exhibit the violence that allegedly led to his death on March 1, 2009.
Speaking on Wednesday afternoon to a Coroner's Inquest into Derek's shooting by RCMP officers nearly two years ago, Carroll Welton recalled an altercation between Derek and his brother, John.
"Derek seemed like he wasn't himself," Carroll told the court. "He struck John, and I grabbed him and held him back."
Other than that, said Carroll, Derek was good-natured when he wasn't on illicit drugs. Two friends of Derek's who also testified Wednesday, also described him that way.
"He was always happy, always in a good mood, always willing to help," said Corey Orcutt.

Orcutt met Derek Welton through Alcoholics Anonymous, he explained. They were sober at the time, but relapsed into using crack cocaine some time later, including smoking it together the morning of Welton's death.

Orcutt called Welton an "amazing person," but noted that "he would change" when he used crack. Most of the time, the two would part ways after smoking, but on one occasion, Orcutt found himself trapped in Welton's trailer for six hours, unable to answer his phone or even stand up during that period of time.
"He became a different person," said Orcutt, who has now been clean for several months and is living in Victoria.

During the initial investigation into the shooting, Orcutt told police that the first time he and Welton had used crack together was the most fearful he had been of anyone in his life. He retracted that statement somewhat at the inquest, but said it was "top five, for sure." He had also told police that drugs made Welton "absolutely mentally insane."
"It makes me feel bad to say that," he said on Thursday.

Another friend, Lisa Kryschuk, was added to the list of witnesses on the last day of testimony. She called Derek Welton a "bubbly, happy man" and a "great guy." She knew about his drug use, but didn't see him when he was using. Kryschuk saw him about two or three days before his death. He looked healthy, she said, but mentioned having trouble with his girlfriend and made an ominous statement. "Something bad is going to happen," he told her.
Kryschuk said she expected to see him sometime the following weekend, but it was on that Sunday that he was shot.
Carroll Welton recalled bringing Derek to Duncan in 1984, the year after his mother passed away. Her death was "devastating" to the then-14-year-old, said Carroll.
"Him and his mother were very close," said the father.

Carroll described how Derek found a job at a local restaurant, but then descended into drinking and taking drugs around the age of 17. He left his father's home at a young age, but remained close with the family. He went on to work for a tree-topping company and then for BC Hydro. In recent years, Carroll continued to see his son regularly.
"I'd see him lots, and when I didn't see him, I'd drop by the trailer," he said.

On at least two occasions while Carroll was visiting Derek, the RCMP came by, only to find out that there wasn't an emergency. Carroll believed someone was making 9-1-1 calls directing police to Derek's trailer.
"I said to Derek, 'someone is setting you up,'" he remembered.
Speaking outside the courthouse, Carroll said that Derek's death and the inquest had been "a trying thing for everybody involved."
"The police have a hard job to do," he said. "We know that it's sometimes necessary. I don't know if the jury will agree or not that use of force was necessary."

Welton had spent time in the Forensic Psychiatric Hospital in Port Coquitlam. Dr. Emlene Murphy, one of his treating psychiatrists there, told the inquest on Wednesday morning that a review board had discharged Welton against her advice.
As a result she took what she called the "atypical" measure of writing to North Cowichan/ Duncan RCMP to alert them of Welton's return to the community.
"What we expected was another crisis or standoff because that was the pattern before," she said. "Morally I think we have to let people know if we think something would happen."

Murphy understood Welton was given an absolute discharge and therefore had no obligation to the justice system but she worried for his health and to facilitate a "smooth transition" offered Welton some options for a halfway-house type of setting on the Mainland or in Victoria. Upon his discharge, however, he opted to return to Duncan.
The issue with that, said the doctor, was that he had no medical supports in the area and wasn't keen to deal with Victoria-based care.
The problem with having Welton involuntarily hospitalized wasn't so much that he didn't fit the criteria, but there wasn't an appropriate bed for him, said Murphy.

"It's simply a question of availability of services," she said, noting most certifications occur through the emergency room but "there's a continuous pressure to get people discharged because it's the only way to deal with incoming patients."

Vancouver Police Department Sgt. Brad Fawcett, a use-of-force expert testified Tuesday afternoon he wasn't surprised police hadn't discussed an exit plan when they went into Welton's trailer on the day he was shot.

"In a perfect world you would like to have strategies for egress as well as penetration and control," he said. In a dynamic police situation, he added, "you're asking quite a lot of a human being to \[plan\]."
Fawcett added the assumption by any group of officers going into a dangerous situation is to leave as a team with the object of interest in custody.
Fawcett also panned Presiding Coroner Rodrick MacKenzie's idea that a bean bag shotgun would have been useful, saying they aren't reliable.

"If you're dealing with somebody that is willing to ignore pain, or is not feeling pain today then it's not going to work," he said. "Somebody with a mental illness or using drugs may have no pain. A lot of those intermediate weapons have significant limitations when you're dealing with people in those categories."
Fawcett also said for Sgt. Greg Pask, the officer who shot Welton, to retreat after firing one shot at the charging man, would have been unwise.
"Someone moving forward moves four to six times faster than one moving backwards," he said. "I wouldn't turn my back to a known threat."

The seven-member jury was sequestered Thursday morning. Their goal was to come up with suggestions on how to prevent a similar event from occurring. The jury had not come forward with their recommendations by press time.
